senses: A gaseous ozone-depleting refrigerant.
A chlorofluorocarbon.
ety: A genericization of the Chemours trademark "Freon." According to Flood, the name was formed from freeze and the arbitrary suffix -on.

senses: An ecofreak.
examples: In the late 1980s and early 1990s, enviros cooked up a scheme to prevent nearly any tree from being cut down in the Pacific Northwest.
The book became one of the enviros’ bibles, and they managed to convince the EPA to ban the use of DDT in the United States in 1972.

senses: A writer, regarded as producing a work but not as providing its explanation (which is instead determined by the reader), according to the theories of Roland Barthes.
ety: From Latin scrīptor, to avoid the etymological link between author and authority.
examples: Although this literary exercise has been used to question the validity of Drew's book, the little biographies he offered acquire a worthy literary dimension if read using Foucault's critique to the Barthesian scriptor.

senses: Severity or strictness.
Harshness, as of climate.
Character of being unyielding or inflexible.
Shrewd questioning.
Higher level of difficulty.
ety: From Middle English rigour, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French rigor, from Latin rigor (“stiffness, rigidity, rigor, cold, harshness”), from rigere (“to be rigid”). Compare French rigueur.

senses: Thinly sliced raw, or lightly cooked bonito, tuna or beef.
That promotes haemostasis
Ramen (Korean style).
ety: Borrowed from Korean 라면 (ramyeon), from Japanese ラーメン (rāmen), from Mandarin 拉麵 /拉面 (lāmiàn, “pulled noodles”). Doublet of laghman, lamian, and ramen.
examples: Anyone can follow the directions on the back of the ramyeon package to boil water and sprinkle in the spice packet, but connoisseurs will add extras like canned tuna, eggs, and cheese for enhanced flavor.

senses: Suddenly, abruptly.
The abstract capability of being programmable.
Somewhat okay; tolerable.
To use such a device or machine
Going on foot; walking.
A form of competitive walking of the nineteenth century, often professional and funded by wagering, from which the modern sport of racewalking developed.
Something that is pedestrian, or banal; a commonplace.
The act of covering the nipples and areolae with the hands, sometimes used for modesty in photographic poses.
A small car used as a taxi (rather than a traditional black cab).
Synonym of gypsy cab, an unlicensed taxi.
Champagne (wine).
A circular design of swirling water, commonly used in Japanese family crests and corporation logos.
An expression of lamentation or complaint.
A medieval dagger, used for the mercy stroke to a wounded foe; misericord.
A small projecting boss or bracket on the underside of the hinged seat of a church stall, intended to give some support to a standing worshipper when the seat is turned up; a misericord.
ety: From Middle English miserere, a borrowing from Latin miserēre (“have pity”), first word of the 51st Psalm (50th in the older Greek and Latin numbering), translating Ancient Greek ἐλέησον (eléēson) and Biblical Hebrew חָנֵּנִי (ḥānnēnî), inflected form of חָנַן (ḥānan, “have mercy”).

senses: The tenure that a man is entitled to over the property of his deceased wife if there is a child who could inherit it.
ety: A variant of courtesy with a specialised sense.

senses: To entangle; to complicate; to involve in knots.
To become entangled.
To place in an embarrassing situation; to ensnare; to make overly complicated.
To be congested in traffic, or to make traffic congested.
To form raised work upon the outer surface of (thin metal ware) by the repercussion of a snarling iron upon the inner surface; to repoussé
ety: From Middle English snarlen, frequentative of snaren (“to trap, tangle”). Equivalent to snare + -le.

senses: A bent pipe or tube with one end lower than the other, in which hydrostatic pressure exerted due to the force of gravity moves liquid from one reservoir to another.
A soda siphon.
ety: From Middle French siphon, from Old French sifon, from Latin sīphō, from Ancient Greek σίφων (síphōn, “pipe, tube”), of uncertain origin; possibly related to Latin tibia (“pipe, flute of bone”), with the irregular forms suggesting a non-Indo-European loan source, perhaps of the shape *twi-, *twibh.

senses: Cheap; inferior.
examples: And now he's made The Number 23, a cheapie $30 million horror film about a man consumed with numerology.

senses: A dish at a restaurant, etc. intended to be shared between several people.
examples: Can we order the seafood platter as a sharer?

senses: A small burrowing rodent native to North and Central America, especially in the family Geomyidae (pocket gophers).
A ground squirrel (Marmotinae spp.).
A gopher tortoise (Gopherus spp.).
A gopher rockfish (Sebastes carnatus).
ety: Perhaps an adaptation of Cajun French gaufre (literally “honeycomb, waffle”), based on the analogy of holes in the ground to the indentations in a honeycomb or a waffle (doublet of waffle). Alternatively, from Muskogean.

senses: The fifteenth day after a feast day, including both days in the reckoning.
A piece of verse having fifteen syllables.
Clothing to be worn while skiing.
A practitioner of obscurantism; an obscurant.
examples: The ego thinks that his local time and space is all there is to reality, and that the busy affairs of state and trade are more important than a lot of obscurantist hocus-pocus.

senses: A person who is neither a citizen nor colonial/imperial subject of the state whose military they join.
A member of a legion, especially the French Foreign Legion.
ety: Borrowed from French légionnaire. Doublet of legionary.

senses: Basics or fundamentals, considered as a unit.
Understanding.
ety: Contraction of fundamental, originating in Indian English.
examples: Get your funda correct before you submit the paper.
What is the funda behind relativity?
You did not have the funda to realize that the statistics is an ass.

senses: A person involved in counterespionage.
The study of cities, their geographic, economic, political, social, and cultural environment.
The culture or way of life of people who live in cities.
Urbanization.
Urban planning.
One of the cabalistic aspects of the soul, related to natural instinct.
An early German form of opera consisting of spoken dialogue interspersed with song.
An opera in this style.
A crossing or intersection of lines etc. so as to form an X-shape.
An animal, such as a bull elephant or a boar, with large tusks.
examples: By climbing trees they had had a fairly good view of the herd, which they described as numbering several large tuskers, a great many cows and calves, and full-grown bulls whose ivory would be worth having.
The massive tusker leading the herd stopped in his tracks. His ears went out, his long sinuous trunk up.

senses: The act of abolishing; abolition; destruction.
ety: From Middle French abolissement, from aboliss-, stem of some conjugated forms abolir, equivalent to abolish + -ment.

senses: Roads sealed with bitumen, as opposed to dirt roads.
Canadian deposits of extremely heavy crude oil.
ety: From Middle English bithumen, bitumen, from Latin bitūmen. Doublet of bitume.

senses: A toothed machine for shredding cellulose in the manufacture of synthetic materials.
Having an external cause, or source; exogenous.
A slick salesman or spin doctor.
examples: A flashman just naturally tried to promote and show- off his company at every opportunity. Wasn't that what sales-PR was all about? Even the police departments engaged flashmen.

senses: The proportion of games played that are won by a given player.
